reference.source: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry; DSM-5-TR
clinicalPearls: Develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, whether directly experienced, witnessed, or learned about affecting a close other
Core symptom clusters are intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares, distressing memories), avoidance of trauma reminders, negative alterations in mood and cognition, and heightened arousal and reactivity
Symptoms persist beyond about one month and cause significant distress or impairment; an acute stress reaction is the label used within the first month
Hyperarousal features include hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, irritability, sleep disturbance, and concentration problems
Trauma-focused psychotherapies (such as trauma-focused CBT and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing) are first-line treatments
Pharmacotherapy principles favour SSRIs or SNRIs; prazosin may help trauma-related nightmares, and benzodiazepines are generally avoided
Screen for common comorbidities including depression, substance use, and suicidal ideation, and for traumatic brain injury in relevant populations
Dissociative symptoms and delayed onset (months to years after the event) are recognised presentations
reference.pathophysiology: Post-traumatic stress disorder reflects dysregulated fear processing, with exaggerated amygdala responses, impaired prefrontal inhibition, and hippocampal changes affecting contextual memory, alongside altered hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and noradrenergic stress responses. These changes underpin persistent conditioned fear, impaired extinction of trauma memories, and chronic hyperarousal.
additionalDifferentials: Panic disorder and other anxiety disorders
Psychosis when flashbacks are mistaken for hallucinations
additionalInvestigations: Structured trauma history and PTSD symptom rating scales
Screening for comorbid depression and substance use
Assessment for traumatic brain injury where relevant
Evaluation of sleep disturbance and nightmares
redFlags: Severe dissociative episodes with risk to safety
Escalating substance or alcohol use to cope with symptoms
Aggression or risk to others during flashbacks or heightened arousal
reference.prognosis: Many people recover within the first year, especially with early trauma-focused treatment, but a substantial minority develop a chronic course. Prognosis is worse with severe or prolonged trauma, lack of social support, and comorbid depression or substance use.
pitfalls: Using benzodiazepines, which do not treat core symptoms and may impair recovery
Missing comorbid depression, substance use, and suicide risk
Overlooking delayed-onset presentations by not taking a trauma history
Mislabelling normal early stress reactions as PTSD before the required duration
Failing to refer for evidence-based trauma-focused psychotherapy
